name: chemistry_set2_p1
label: Chemistry: set 2 (acids, salts, solutions, redox and physical chemistry)

papers.title: Acids, Bases, and pH: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on acids, bases, and ph, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: According to the Brønsted–Lowry theory, an acid is
questions.explanation:
In HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻, HCl donates a proton to water, so HCl is the acid and water is the base.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a proton (H⁺) acceptor: That is a Brønsted–Lowry base.
- an electron-pair donor: That is a Lewis base.
- a substance that produces OH⁻ ions in water: That is the Arrhenius definition of a base (alkali).

options.label: D
options.content: a substance that produces OH⁻ ions in water

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.01 mol/dm³ solution of hydrochloric acid (fully ionised)?
questions.explanation:
$[\text{H}^+] = 0.01 = 10^{-2}$ mol/dm³, so pH $= -\log 10^{-2} = 2$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.01: That is the hydrogen ion concentration, not the pH.
- −2: pH = −log[H⁺]; you left out the minus sign.
- 12: That would be the pH of 0.01 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide.

questions.stem: Ethanoic acid is described as a weak acid because it
questions.explanation:
Only about 1% of ethanoic acid molecules ionise in a 0.1 mol/dm³ solution: CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- is always dilute: Weak and dilute mean different things; concentrated ethanoic acid is still weak.
- does not react with metals: Ethanoic acid reacts (slowly) with reactive metals such as magnesium.
- contains few hydrogen atoms: Strength depends on ionisation, not on the number of hydrogen atoms.

options.label: A
options.content: is only partially ionised in water

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.001 mol/dm³ solution of sodium hydroxide? (pH + pOH = 14)
questions.explanation:
$[\text{OH}^-] = 10^{-3}$, so pOH $= 3$ and pH $= 14 - 3 = 11$.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 3: That is the pOH, not the pH.
- 0.001: That is the hydroxide ion concentration.
- 4: You subtracted 3 from 7 instead of finding 14 − pOH.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an amphoteric oxide?
questions.explanation:
An amphoteric oxide reacts with both acids and alkalis: ZnO + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂O and ZnO + 2NaOH → Na₂ZnO₂ + H₂O.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Sodium oxide: Sodium oxide is basic: it reacts only with acids.
- Sulphur(IV) oxide: Sulphur(IV) oxide is acidic: it reacts with alkalis.
- Carbon(II) oxide: Carbon(II) oxide is neutral: it reacts with neither acids nor alkalis.

papers.title: Salts and Their Preparation: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on salts and their preparation, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which salt is best prepared by precipitation (double decomposition)?
questions.explanation:
Insoluble salts are made by mixing two soluble salts: Pb(NO₃)₂ + 2KI → PbI₂(s) + 2KNO₃, then filtering and washing.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Sodium nitrate: Sodium nitrate is soluble; it is made by titrating an acid with an alkali.
- Copper(II) sulphate: It is soluble; it is made by adding excess copper(II) oxide to the acid.
- Magnesium chloride: It is soluble; it is made by adding excess magnesium to the acid.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an acid salt?
questions.explanation:
An acid salt still contains replaceable hydrogen; NaHSO₄ is formed when only one H of H₂SO₄ is replaced.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Na₂SO₄: Na₂SO₄ is a normal salt: all the replaceable hydrogen has been replaced.
- Mg(OH)Cl: Mg(OH)Cl is a basic salt; it contains hydroxide.
- KAl(SO₄)₂·12H₂O: Potash alum is a double salt.

questions.stem: Solid sodium hydroxide left in an open dish absorbs water from the air and dissolves in it. It is described as
questions.explanation:
Deliquescent substances (NaOH, CaCl₂, MgCl₂) absorb so much water that they form a solution.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- efflorescent: Efflorescent crystals lose water of crystallisation to the air.
- hygroscopic: Hygroscopic substances absorb water but do not dissolve in it.
- hydrated: Hydrated means containing water of crystallisation.

questions.stem: When copper(II) sulphate is made from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulphuric acid, excess copper(II) oxide is added in order to
questions.explanation:
The unreacted solid oxide is filtered off, leaving a solution of the salt with no acid left in it.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- speed up the crystallisation: Excess oxide does not affect crystallisation; it is filtered off first.
- make the solution more acidic: Excess base removes acid; it does not add any.
- increase the solubility of the salt: The amount of base added does not change solubility.

options.label: C
options.content: increase the solubility of the salt

options.label: D
options.content: make sure that all the acid is used up

questions.stem: What mass of copper(II) sulphate crystals, CuSO₄·5H₂O, can be made from 0.05 mol of sulphuric acid? (CuSO₄·5H₂O = 250)
questions.explanation:
1 mol H₂SO₄ gives 1 mol CuSO₄·5H₂O, so mass $= 0.05 \times 250 = 12.5$ g.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 8 g: That is the mass of anhydrous CuSO₄ (Mᵣ 160); the crystals contain water.
- 4.9 g: That is the mass of the sulphuric acid used (Mᵣ 98).
- 250 g: That is the molar mass; multiply it by the number of moles.

papers.title: Acid-Base Titration: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on acid-base titration, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid. What is the concentration of the sodium hydroxide?
questions.explanation:
Moles HCl $= 0.100 \times \dfrac{20.0}{1000} = 0.00200$; ratio 1 : 1; $[\text{NaOH}] = \dfrac{0.00200}{0.0250} = 0.0800$ mol/dm³

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.125 mol/dm³: You inverted the volumes.
- 0.002 mol/dm³: That is the number of moles, not the concentration.
- 0.1 mol/dm³: The volumes are different, so the concentrations cannot be equal.

questions.stem: 25.0 cm³ of sodium carbonate solution needs 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ HCl for complete reaction: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. What is the concentration of the sodium carbonate?
questions.explanation:
Moles HCl $= 0.00200$; moles Na₂CO₃ $= \dfrac{0.00200}{2} = 0.00100$; concentration $= \dfrac{0.00100}{0.0250} = 0.0400$ mol/dm³

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.08 mol/dm³: You used a 1 : 1 ratio; 1 mol Na₂CO₃ reacts with 2 mol HCl.
- 0.16 mol/dm³: You multiplied by 2 instead of dividing by 2.
- 0.001 mol/dm³: That is the number of moles of Na₂CO₃, not its concentration.

questions.stem: Which indicator is most suitable for titrating ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide solution?
questions.explanation:
The end point of a weak acid–strong base titration is above pH 7, which matches phenolphthalein's range (8–10).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Methyl orange: Methyl orange changes at pH 3–4.5, before the end point of a weak acid–strong base titration.
- Litmus: Litmus changes colour gradually and is not used for accurate titrations.
- Universal indicator: Universal indicator gives a range of colours, not a sharp end point.

questions.stem: What colour is methyl orange in an alkaline solution?
questions.explanation:
Methyl orange: red in acid, orange at the end point, yellow in alkali.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Red: Methyl orange is red in acidic solution.
- Pink: Pink is the colour of phenolphthalein in alkali.
- Colourless: Phenolphthalein, not methyl orange, is colourless in acid.

questions.stem: Three accurate titres were 23.80 cm³, 23.90 cm³ and 24.40 cm³. What average titre should be used in the calculation?
questions.explanation:
Concordant titres agree within 0.10 cm³: 23.80 and 23.90. Average $= \dfrac{23.80 + 23.90}{2} = 23.85$ cm³

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 24.03 cm³: You averaged all three; 24.40 is not concordant and must be left out.
- 24.40 cm³: That is the result that disagrees with the others.
- 23.80 cm³: That is only the smallest titre.

papers.title: Water and Its Properties: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on water and its properties, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Temporary hardness of water is caused by dissolved
questions.explanation:
Boiling decomposes calcium hydrogencarbonate: Ca(HCO₃)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O + CO₂, removing the Ca²⁺ ions.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- calcium sulphate: Calcium sulphate causes permanent hardness.
- sodium chloride: Sodium ions do not cause hardness.
- magnesium chloride: Magnesium chloride causes permanent hardness.

questions.stem: Permanent hardness of water can be removed by
questions.explanation:
Carbonate ions precipitate the hardness ions: Ca²⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → CaCO₃(s). Ion exchange and distillation also work.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- boiling: Boiling removes only temporary hardness.
- filtration: The hardness ions are dissolved, so they pass through a filter.
- adding chlorine: Chlorine kills germs; it does not remove calcium or magnesium ions.

questions.stem: Which test shows that a liquid contains water?
questions.explanation:
These tests show that water is present; to show it is pure water, check that it boils at 100 °C and freezes at 0 °C.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- It turns blue litmus paper red: That shows the liquid is acidic.
- It turns lime water milky: That is the test for carbon(IV) oxide.
- It turns pink cobalt(II) chloride paper blue: The change is the other way: water turns blue cobalt(II) chloride paper pink.

options.label: A
options.content: It turns white anhydrous copper(II) sulphate blue

options.label: B
options.content: It turns blue litmus paper red

options.label: D
options.content: It turns pink cobalt(II) chloride paper blue

questions.stem: In the treatment of a town's water supply, chlorine is added to
questions.explanation:
Chlorine (or chlorine compounds) disinfects the water so that diseases such as cholera and typhoid are not spread.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- make suspended particles settle: Alum (aluminium sulphate) is added to coagulate fine particles.
- remove dissolved salts: Chlorine does not remove dissolved salts.
- remove unpleasant smells by aeration: Aeration is done by spraying the water into air.

questions.stem: Ice floats on liquid water because
questions.explanation:
Water is densest at 4 °C. On freezing, hydrogen bonding forms an open lattice, so ice is about 9% less dense than water.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- ice contains trapped air: Pure ice floats even with no air in it.
- ice molecules are lighter than water molecules: The molecules are identical H₂O.
- ice has a lower boiling point: Boiling point has nothing to do with floating.

options.label: B
options.content: ice molecules are lighter than water molecules

options.label: C
options.content: hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open structure, so ice is less dense

options.label: D
options.content: ice has a lower boiling point

papers.title: Solutions and Solubility: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on solutions and solubility, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: At 25 °C, 12 g of a salt dissolves in 40 g of water to form a saturated solution. What is the solubility of the salt in g per 100 g of water?
questions.explanation:
Solubility $= \dfrac{12}{40} \times 100 = 30$ g per 100 g of water.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 12 g: That is the mass dissolved in 40 g of water, not in 100 g.
- 4.8 g: You multiplied by 40 and divided by 100 instead of the reverse.
- 33.33 g: You divided 40 by 12.

questions.stem: The solubility of salt X is 80 g per 100 g of water at 60 °C and 30 g per 100 g at 20 °C. What mass of crystals forms when a saturated solution in 100 g of water is cooled from 60 °C to 20 °C?
questions.explanation:
Mass of crystals $= 80 - 30 = 50$ g

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 110 g: You added the two solubilities.
- 80 g: Not all the salt comes out; 30 g stays dissolved at 20 °C.
- 30 g: That is the mass that stays in solution.

questions.stem: As the temperature of water rises, the solubility of gases such as oxygen in it
questions.explanation:
Gas molecules gain energy and escape from warm water; this is why warm water from factories (thermal pollution) holds less oxygen for fish.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- increases: That is true of most solids, not gases.
- stays the same: Gas solubility changes noticeably with temperature.
- first increases and then decreases: Gas solubility falls steadily as temperature rises.

questions.stem: A saturated solution is one that
questions.explanation:
At a given temperature, no more solute will dissolve in a saturated solution; extra solid stays undissolved.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- contains a very large amount of solute: A solution of a sparingly soluble salt can be saturated yet very dilute.
- has been heated to its boiling point: Saturation has nothing to do with boiling.
- contains two or more solutes: Saturation refers to one solute reaching its limit.

options.label: A
options.content: contains as much solute as can dissolve at that temperature

options.label: B
options.content: contains a very large amount of solute

options.label: C
options.content: has been heated to its boiling point

questions.stem: A beam of light passed through starch solution is visible from the side, but not when passed through salt solution. This is
questions.explanation:
Colloid particles (1–1000 nm) are big enough to scatter light; the ions in a true solution are too small.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Brownian motion: Brownian motion is the random movement of small particles in a fluid.
- dialysis: Dialysis separates colloid particles from small ions through a membrane.
- coagulation: Coagulation is the clumping together of colloid particles.

papers.title: Oxidation and Reduction Reactions: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on oxidation and reduction reactions, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of manganese in potassium manganate(VII), KMnO₄?
questions.explanation:
K is +1 and each O is −2: +1 + x − 8 = 0, so x = +7, as the name manganate(VII) shows.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- +6: Check the sum: +1 + x + 4(−2) = 0 gives x = +7.
- +4: +4 is manganese's oxidation number in MnO₂.
- +2: +2 is manganese's oxidation number in Mn²⁺ salts.

questions.stem: In the reaction Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, the reducing agent is
questions.explanation:
Zinc loses two electrons (it is oxidised) and gives them to Cu²⁺; the substance that gives electrons is the reducing agent.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Cu²⁺: Cu²⁺ gains electrons: it is the oxidising agent.
- Zn²⁺: Zn²⁺ is a product, formed when zinc is oxidised.
- Cu: Cu is a product, formed when Cu²⁺ is reduced.

questions.stem: In terms of electron transfer, oxidation is
questions.explanation:
OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss of electrons; Reduction Is Gain. Oxidation also means an increase in oxidation number.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the gain of electrons: That is reduction (OIL RIG: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain).
- the gain of protons: Proton transfer describes acid–base reactions.
- the loss of oxygen: Loss of oxygen is reduction.

questions.stem: Which change is a reduction?
questions.explanation:
Fe³⁺ gains one electron and its oxidation number falls from +3 to +2: that is reduction.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺: The oxidation number rises from +2 to +3: oxidation.
- 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂: Chloride ions lose electrons: oxidation.
- Cu → Cu²⁺: Copper loses electrons: oxidation.

questions.stem: Which observation shows that a gas is a reducing agent?
questions.explanation:
The gas reduces orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ (Cr +6) to green Cr³⁺ (Cr +3); sulphur(IV) oxide and hydrogen sulphide do this.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- It turns lime water milky: That is the test for carbon(IV) oxide, which is not acting as a reducing agent.
- It relights a glowing splint: That shows oxygen, which supports burning.
- It turns damp red litmus paper blue: That shows an alkaline gas (ammonia).

options.label: B
options.content: It turns acidified potassium dichromate(VI) from orange to green

options.label: D
options.content: It turns damp red litmus paper blue

papers.title: Electrolysis: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on electrolysis, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: In the electrolysis of concentrated sodium chloride solution with carbon electrodes, the product at the anode is
questions.explanation:
Concentrated Cl⁻ ions are discharged in preference to OH⁻ at the anode: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- oxygen: Oxygen forms at the anode only with dilute chloride solutions.
- hydrogen: Hydrogen is formed at the cathode.
- sodium: Sodium is never formed from aqueous solution; it would react with water.

questions.stem: What mass of copper is deposited at the cathode when 9650 C of electricity passes through copper(II) sulphate solution? (Cu = 64; F = 96 500 C/mol)
questions.explanation:
Moles of electrons $= \dfrac{9650}{96\,500} = 0.1$; Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, so moles Cu $= 0.05$; mass $= 0.05 \times 64 = 3.2$ g

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 6.4 g: You used one electron per copper ion; Cu²⁺ needs two.
- 0.05 g: That is the number of moles of copper, not its mass.
- 1.6 g: You divided by 4 instead of 2.

questions.stem: In the electrolysis of dilute sulphuric acid, oxygen forms at the anode: 4OH⁻ → 2H₂O + O₂ + 4e⁻. What volume of oxygen at s.t.p. is produced by 0.4 mol of electrons?
questions.explanation:
Moles O₂ $= \dfrac{0.4}{4} = 0.1$; volume $= 0.1 \times 22.4 = 2.24$ dm³

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 4.48 dm³: You used two electrons per O₂; four are needed.
- 8.96 dm³: You assumed one mole of O₂ per mole of electrons.
- 2.4 dm³: You used 24 dm³, the molar volume at room conditions.

questions.stem: In the purification of copper by electrolysis, the impure copper is made the
questions.explanation:
At the anode, copper dissolves as Cu²⁺; the ions move to the cathode and are deposited as pure copper. Impurities fall as anode sludge.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- cathode: Pure copper is deposited on the cathode.
- electrolyte: The electrolyte is copper(II) sulphate solution.
- salt bridge: There is no salt bridge in an electrolytic cell.

questions.stem: Sodium is extracted by electrolysing molten sodium chloride, not its aqueous solution, because in aqueous solution
questions.explanation:
Water's H⁺ ions are discharged more easily than Na⁺; and any sodium formed would react with water at once.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- sodium chloride does not conduct electricity: Aqueous sodium chloride is a good electrolyte.
- chlorine would not be formed: Chlorine is formed at the anode from concentrated solution.
- the solution would be too expensive: Cost is not the reason; the chemistry is.

options.label: A
options.content: hydrogen is discharged at the cathode instead of sodium

options.label: B
options.content: sodium chloride does not conduct electricity

options.label: D
options.content: the solution would be too expensive

papers.title: Electrochemical Cells: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on electrochemical cells, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: E° for Zn²⁺/Zn is −0.76 V and for Cu²⁺/Cu is +0.34 V. What is the e.m.f. of the Daniell cell?
questions.explanation:
$E_{\text{cell}} = E_{\text{right}} - E_{\text{left}} = +0.34 - (-0.76) = +1.10$ V

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.42 V: You subtracted the sizes without the signs: 0.76 − 0.34.
- −0.42 V: You added the two potentials.
- −1.10 V: You subtracted the wrong way round; a working cell has a positive e.m.f.

questions.stem: In the Daniell cell, electrons flow in the external wire
questions.explanation:
Zinc is oxidised (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻) and is the negative electrode; electrons travel to the copper, where Cu²⁺ is reduced.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- from the copper electrode to the zinc electrode: Zinc is more reactive, so it gives up electrons.
- through the salt bridge: Ions, not electrons, move through the salt bridge.
- in both directions equally: The current flows one way while the cell discharges.

options.label: A
options.content: from the copper electrode to the zinc electrode

options.label: B
options.content: from the zinc electrode to the copper electrode

questions.stem: The function of the salt bridge in a cell is to
questions.explanation:
Ions in the salt bridge keep each solution electrically neutral, so current can continue to flow.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- carry electrons between the electrodes: Electrons flow through the external wire, not the salt bridge.
- increase the e.m.f. of the cell: The salt bridge does not change the e.m.f.
- supply the metal ions that are reduced: The metal ions come from the electrolyte in each half-cell.

options.label: B
options.content: increase the e.m.f. of the cell

options.label: C
options.content: complete the circuit by allowing ions to move between the half-cells

options.label: D
options.content: supply the metal ions that are reduced

questions.stem: In the zinc–carbon dry (Leclanché) cell, the electrolyte is
questions.explanation:
The dry cell has a zinc case (negative), a carbon rod (positive) surrounded by MnO₂, and a moist NH₄Cl paste as electrolyte.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- dilute sulphuric acid: That is the electrolyte of the lead–acid accumulator.
- manganese(IV) oxide: Manganese(IV) oxide is the depolariser around the carbon rod.
- zinc: The zinc case is the negative electrode.

questions.stem: Galvanised iron does not rust even when the zinc coating is scratched because zinc
questions.explanation:
This is sacrificial protection: zinc loses electrons more readily than iron, so the iron stays reduced.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- is less reactive than iron: A less reactive coating (such as tin) makes rusting faster when scratched.
- forms an airtight layer over the scratch: The scratch exposes the iron; protection is sacrificial.
- reacts with rust to form iron: Zinc does not reverse rusting.

options.label: A
options.content: is more reactive than iron and corrodes in preference to it

options.label: C
options.content: forms an airtight layer over the scratch

options.label: D
options.content: reacts with rust to form iron

papers.title: Energy Changes in Reactions: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on energy changes in reactions, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: In an exothermic reaction
questions.explanation:
The products have less energy than the reactants; the difference is released to the surroundings, which get warmer.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- heat is taken in and ΔH is negative: Heat taken in means ΔH is positive (endothermic).
- heat is given out and ΔH is positive: When heat is given out, the products have less energy, so ΔH is negative.
- heat is taken in and ΔH is positive: That describes an endothermic reaction.

options.label: A
options.content: heat is taken in and ΔH is negative

options.label: B
options.content: heat is given out and ΔH is negative

options.label: C
options.content: heat is given out and ΔH is positive

options.label: D
options.content: heat is taken in and ΔH is positive

questions.stem: A reaction raises the temperature of 50 g of solution by 6 °C. How much heat is given out? (c = 4.2 J/g/°C)
questions.explanation:
$Q = mc\Delta T = 50 \times 4.2 \times 6 = 1260$ J

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 210 J: You left out the temperature change.
- 300 J: You left out the specific heat capacity.
- 25.2 J: You left out the mass.

questions.stem: 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ HCl is mixed with 50 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ NaOH, and the temperature rises by 6.8 °C. What is the enthalpy of neutralisation? (Mass of solution = 100 g; c = 4.2 J/g/°C)
questions.explanation:
$Q = 100 \times 4.2 \times 6.8 = 2856$ J; moles of water $= 0.05$; $\Delta H = -\dfrac{2.856}{0.05} = -57.12$ kJ/mol

**Why the other options are wrong**

- −28.56 kJ/mol: You used only 50 g; the mass of the whole mixture is 100 g.
- −2.856 kJ/mol: That is the heat released in kJ; divide by the 0.05 mol of water formed.
- 57.12 kJ/mol: Neutralisation gives out heat, so ΔH is negative.

questions.stem: Use the bond energies H–H = 436, Cl–Cl = 242 and H–Cl = 431 kJ/mol to find ΔH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl.
questions.explanation:
Bonds broken $= 436 + 242 = 678$; bonds made $= 2 \times 431 = 862$; $\Delta H = 678 - 862 = -184$ kJ/mol

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 184 kJ/mol: You subtracted the bonds broken from the bonds made; ΔH = bonds broken − bonds made.
- 247 kJ/mol: You formed only one H–Cl bond; two are formed.
- −1540 kJ/mol: You added all the bond energies and made the total negative.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an endothermic process?
questions.explanation:
The solution gets colder as ammonium nitrate dissolves, because heat is taken in from the surroundings.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Burning methane: Combustion always gives out heat.
- Neutralising an acid with an alkali: Neutralisation is exothermic (about −57 kJ/mol).
- Respiration: Respiration releases energy from glucose.

options.label: B
options.content: Neutralising an acid with an alkali

papers.title: Rate of Reaction: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on rate of reaction, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Raising the temperature increases the rate of a reaction mainly because
questions.explanation:
Faster particles collide more often, and a much larger fraction of collisions have enough energy to react.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the activation energy is lowered: Temperature does not change the activation energy; a catalyst does.
- the particles become larger: Particle size does not change with temperature.
- the concentration of the reactants increases: Heating does not change concentration.

options.label: C
options.content: the concentration of the reactants increases

options.label: D
options.content: more particles have energy equal to or greater than the activation energy

questions.stem: Powdered marble reacts faster with dilute hydrochloric acid than the same mass of marble lumps because the powder
questions.explanation:
More particles are exposed to the acid, so there are more collisions per second.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- has a lower activation energy: Both forms are the same substance with the same activation energy.
- is more concentrated: Concentration applies to solutions, not to the solid.
- contains more calcium carbonate: The masses are the same.

questions.stem: A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction by
questions.explanation:
With a lower activation energy, a greater fraction of collisions are successful at the same temperature.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- increasing the energy of the reacting particles: A catalyst does not heat the reactants.
- shifting the equilibrium towards the products: A catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium.
- being used up in the reaction: A catalyst is unchanged chemically at the end.

options.label: A
options.content: increasing the energy of the reacting particles

options.label: B
options.content: providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy

options.label: C
options.content: shifting the equilibrium towards the products

options.label: D
options.content: being used up in the reaction

questions.stem: In the first 30 s of a reaction, 60 cm³ of gas is collected. What is the average rate of the reaction over this time?
questions.explanation:
Average rate $= \dfrac{\text{volume of gas}}{\text{time}} = \dfrac{60}{30} = 2$ cm³/s

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 0.5 cm³/s: You divided the time by the volume.
- 1800 cm³/s: You multiplied instead of dividing.
- 30 cm³/s: You divided the volume by 2 instead of by the time.

questions.stem: On a graph of the volume of gas collected against time, the curve eventually becomes horizontal because
questions.explanation:
When the limiting reactant is used up, no more gas is produced, so the volume stays constant.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the catalyst has been used up: Catalysts are not used up.
- the gas has stopped being collected: The apparatus still collects gas; none is being made.
- the activation energy has increased: The activation energy does not change during the reaction.

options.label: A
options.content: the catalyst has been used up

options.label: B
options.content: the gas has stopped being collected

options.label: C
options.content: one of the reactants has been used up

papers.title: Chemical Equilibrium: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on chemical equilibrium, each with a worked solution and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A reversible reaction is in dynamic equilibrium when
questions.explanation:
Because the rates are equal, the concentrations stop changing even though particles keep reacting both ways.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- both reactions have stopped: At dynamic equilibrium, both reactions continue.
- the concentrations of reactants and products are equal: The concentrations are constant, not necessarily equal.
- all the reactants have been used up: Some reactants always remain at equilibrium.

options.label: B
options.content: the concentrations of reactants and products are equal

options.label: C
options.content: all the reactants have been used up

options.label: D
options.content: the forward and backward reactions continue at equal rates

questions.stem: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), increasing the pressure
questions.explanation:
By Le Chatelier's principle, the system reduces the pressure by shifting to the side with fewer gas molecules.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- decreases the yield of ammonia, because there are fewer gas molecules on the right: Higher pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules.
- has no effect, because all the substances are gases: The number of gas molecules differs: 4 on the left, 2 on the right.
- increases the yield, because the reaction is exothermic: Pressure acts through the number of gas molecules, not through ΔH.

options.label: A
options.content: increases the yield of ammonia, because there are fewer gas molecules on the right

options.label: B
options.content: decreases the yield of ammonia, because there are fewer gas molecules on the right

options.label: C
options.content: has no effect, because all the substances are gases

options.label: D
options.content: increases the yield, because the reaction is exothermic

questions.stem: For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH = −92 kJ/mol, raising the temperature
questions.explanation:
Heating favours the endothermic direction (the backward reaction), so less ammonia is present at equilibrium; it does make equilibrium faster.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- increases the yield of ammonia: The forward reaction is exothermic, so heating favours the backward reaction.
- does not change the yield of ammonia: Temperature changes the position of equilibrium.
- stops the reaction: The reaction continues, faster, at a higher temperature.

options.label: C
options.content: does not change the yield of ammonia

questions.stem: Adding a catalyst to a reaction at equilibrium
questions.explanation:
A catalyst lets equilibrium be reached sooner, but the equilibrium amounts are the same.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- increases the yield of products: A catalyst speeds up both directions equally.
- decreases the yield of products: A catalyst does not favour either direction.
- changes the value of the equilibrium constant: Only temperature changes the equilibrium constant.

options.label: C
options.content: does not change the position of equilibrium

options.label: D
options.content: changes the value of the equilibrium constant

questions.stem: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), the equilibrium concentrations are [H₂] = 0.1, [I₂] = 0.1 and [HI] = 0.8 mol/dm³. What is Kc?
questions.explanation:
$K_c = \dfrac{[\text{HI}]^2}{[\text{H}_2][\text{I}_2]} = \dfrac{0.8^2}{0.1 \times 0.1} = \dfrac{0.64}{0.01} = 64$

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 80: You did not square [HI]; its coefficient is 2.
- 8: You divided by only one of the reactant concentrations and did not square [HI].
- 0.015625: You put the reactants over the products.
